output.summary: Severe aortic stenosis (valve area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak velocity >4.0 m/s) presenting with syncope is a Class I indication for aortic valve intervention per ESC/EACTS 2021 and ACC/AHA guidelines. Syncope in severe AS carries an average 3-year survival without intervention. Exertional syncope requires urgent echocardiographic evaluation to exclude structural causes including AS and HOCM before any neurally mediated testing is considered.

alternatives: Definitive management of AS hemodynamics is surgical AVR or TAVR; antihypertensive medication adjustments are temporizing only

contraindications: Diuretics (thiazides, loop diuretics) are relatively contraindicated in severe AS — excessive preload reduction decreases cardiac output across the fixed obstruction and may precipitate syncope or hemodynamic collapse

interactions: Amlodipine and Lisinopril: systemic vasodilation from either agent can reduce preload and afterload; in fixed-obstruction severe AS this may precipitate hypotension and hemodynamic decompensation as cardiac output cannot augment reflexively through the stenotic valve

Lisinopril: ACE inhibitors cause peripheral vasodilation; in severe AS where stroke volume is relatively fixed, this may worsen hypotension without the compensatory cardiac output increase possible in non-obstructed patients

warnings: Use vasodilators and diuretics with extreme caution in severe AS; hemodynamic effects are poorly tolerated

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform tilt-table testing in confirmed or strongly suspected severe aortic stenosis — hemodynamic collapse risk
Do not perform exercise stress testing in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis — ACC/AHA Class III contraindication
Do not discharge patient home without echocardiographic assessment; exertional syncope from structural cause has high short-term mortality without intervention
Do not attribute exertional syncope in an elderly patient to deconditioning or orthostasis without first completing cardiac structural workup

Do not administer potent vasodilators (nitroglycerin, nitrates, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors) or aggressive diuretics in severe AS — preload reduction across fixed obstruction can precipitate hemodynamic collapse
required_recommendations: Recognize exertional syncope as a high-risk feature mandating urgent cardiac evaluation — do not attribute to deconditioning or orthostasis before structural workup is complete
Identify the harsh late-peaking systolic ejection murmur radiating to carotids with soft S2 and pulsus parvus et tardus as classic signs of severe aortic stenosis
Obtain echocardiogram urgently to confirm severity of aortic stenosis (valve area, mean gradient, peak velocity, LVEF)
Admit to monitored bed with continuous telemetry to exclude concurrent arrhythmia
Consult structural heart team (cardiology and cardiac surgery) for AVR or TAVR evaluation given symptomatic severe AS with syncope
Recognize BNP elevation as reflecting elevated LV filling pressures from pressure overload, consistent with severe AS — not a competing diagnosis
Review and hold or reduce vasodilators and diuretics until definitive valve intervention

avoided_actions.rationale: No focal neurological deficits, no seizure features, and no stroke on differential for the syncopal mechanism; routine brain MRI not indicated in straightforward cardiac syncope evaluation.
No meningismus, fever, encephalopathy, or subarachnoid hemorrhage features; CSF analysis has no role in this cardiac syncope evaluation.
No features of seizure disorder (no post-ictal confusion, no tongue bite, no aura, no convulsive movements); EEG not indicated in straightforward cardiac syncope.
No head trauma requiring hemorrhage exclusion; routine CT head not indicated for cardiac syncope workup.

Tilt-table testing is relatively contraindicated in confirmed severe aortic stenosis; upright positioning provokes venous pooling and reduced preload across a fixed outflow obstruction, risking dangerous hypotension and hemodynamic collapse. It does not add diagnostic information when structural AS is already confirmed and is the presumed mechanism of exertional syncope.

Exercise stress testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (ACC/AHA Class III). It can provoke severe hypotension, syncope, or sudden cardiac death by increasing cardiac output demand across a fixed obstruction that the stenotic valve cannot accommodate.

PE can cause syncope; however, absence of pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, or risk factors, and the presence of a classic murmur point away from PE as the primary etiology.

key_clinical_evidence: Exertional syncope is a high-risk red flag for structural cardiac disease, not a benign finding attributable to deconditioning in the elderly; it mandates urgent cardiac evaluation including echocardiography
A harsh late-peaking systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids with soft S2 and pulsus parvus et tardus constitutes the classic physical examination triad of severe aortic stenosis

Echocardiographic criteria for severe AS (valve area <1.0 cm2, mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak velocity >4.0 m/s) are present and are the diagnostic load-bearing finding; symptomatic severe AS with syncope is a Class I indication for valve intervention
Tilt-table testing and exercise stress testing are both contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS and must not be performed
Normal cardiac telemetry during admission excludes concurrent arrhythmic syncope and reinforces the structural AS mechanism
BNP elevation reflects LV pressure overload from outflow obstruction, consistent with severe AS — it does not constitute a competing diagnosis or redirect the workup

clinical_pearls: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) is the prototypical structural cause of cardiac syncope; the classic symptomatic triad — syncope, angina, and heart failure — each confer high short-term mortality without valve intervention

The physical examination in severe AS is highly specific: harsh late-peaking systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, soft or absent A2, and pulsus parvus et tardus (diminished and delayed carotid upstroke)
Exertional syncope in severe AS results from inability to augment cardiac output across the fixed obstruction during exercise, combined with peripheral vasodilation, causing cerebral hypoperfusion
Tilt-table testing and exercise stress testing are both contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS due to risk of hemodynamic collapse
TAVR has expanded valve replacement options to patients at high or prohibitive surgical risk, making age alone no longer a barrier to intervention in severe symptomatic AS
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Classic straightforward presentation: exertional syncope + diagnostic AS murmur on exam + confirmatory echocardiogram with 3 pathognomonic severe-AS criteria. One grounded red herring (deconditioning misattribution). Diagnosis is clinically clear once echo returns.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Merritt is a 78-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department after suddenly losing consciousness while climbing a flight of stairs at home approximately two hours ago. His wife witnessed the event and reports that he was mid-way up the stairs when he suddenly went pale and slumped against the railing, sliding down two steps before she caught him. He was unresponsive for approximately 20-25 seconds and then regained consciousness. There was no preceding warning, no cry out, no convulsive movements, and no urinary incontinence. He was immediately alert and oriented on awakening, asking his wife what had happened. He denied palpitations or chest pain at any point before or during the event. He has had no prior frank syncopal episodes; however, his wife reports that for approximately 6-8 months he has been gradually stopping activities he used to enjoy, notably daily walks and climbing stairs, because he felt 'light-headed and breathless.' She thought he was just 'getting old' or was 'deconditioned.' On one occasion three months ago he nearly blacked out at the top of the stairs but sat down quickly and recovered. He has also noticed that he becomes short of breath carrying groceries. He denies rest symptoms, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He denies chest pain at rest. He has never been told he has a heart murmur. He has not seen a cardiologist and has never had an echocardiogram.
